GPT-5.5</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The causal chain that runs from weak antitrust to all sorts of social harms </span><em>necessarily runs through profits</em><span>. If companies aren’t making profit, they aren’t controlling the market. Yet Elizabeth Warren blamed high food prices on grocery stores’ market power during the post-pandemic inflation, despite the fact that these stores make very little profit, and their margins </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cd08ead0-9d88-443d-a836-644416d5db55?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">actually declined</a><span> as inflation accelerated. You could see that exact same misplaced focus in Lina Khan’s blockage of the Kroger/Albertsons merger. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As for airlines, the Biden administration’s blockage of the Spirit/JetBlue merger resulted in Spirit Airlines simply </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/424f1e0a-e62a-4520-baeb-1cc602c03d83?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">going out of business entirely</a><span>. Corporate concentration was achieved after all — but it was achieved with disorder, corporate failure, and 17,000 unemployed workers rather than with an orderly merger that would have preserved some of Spirit’s routes and workers. Not exactly a resounding success for the antimonopoly movement — but that’s what happens when you try to use antitrust tools against companies in low-margin industries. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Then there’s the case of housing. The antimonopoly people have eagerly embraced the idea that corporate landlords buying up rental properties and jacking up the price is a major cause of high rent. Democrats and Republicans have </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/23fa3296-003d-4692-9f5e-84ed866ae459?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">both embraced this piece of “slopulism”</a><span>, despite the fact that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45bd5adb-df3d-43ae-945d-311bfbc1c4f8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the percent of homes owned by corporate landlords is tiny</a><span> and there’s some evidence showing that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c6d081cc-1412-444e-904b-94b6075648a2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">corporate landlords tend to charge lower rents</a><span>. Supply constraints — failure to build more housing — is actually the reason for high rents, so the antimonopoly movement is distracting us from solving the real problem. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The movement’s obsessive monomania — its conviction that corporate concentration is the root of all of America’s problems — is causing it to pick the wrong targets and hurt workers. That doesn’t mean bigger corporations are better, or that there aren’t industries where we need stronger antitrust. But the antimonopolists’ totalizing obsession causes them to ignore the evidence of where and when their ideas are needed, because they assume that their ideas are </span><em>always</em><span> the top priority in every situation and should be applied in a blanket way to any target they choose. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The science on monopoly power isn’t settled</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Richard Feynman once said of science that “Of all its many values, the greatest must be the freedom to doubt.” Now you can respond that economics and politics aren’t “science”, but that makes the freedom to doubt even </span><em>more</em><span> important; the less conclusively that any one data set can answer your questions, the more important it is to look at a wide variety of data sets and consider a variety of explanations and theories. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">From Jonathan Chait’s description of Barry C. Lynn, he doesn’t seem like the kind of guy who’s inclined to look at evidence that goes against his ideas:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[Lynn] believes that “most prices are entirely arbitrary and political in nature.”…More expansively, Lynn believes that “market forces”—which he places in scare quotes—do not exist. His indictment of economics is neither mild nor limited. He has compared the discipline to Lysenkoism, a pseudo-scientific fad under Stalin. “The ‘science’ of economics today … ,” he wrote in his 2011 book, </span><em>Cornered</em><span>, “has become a form of madness, a dream of human imagination we mistake for a pattern of the world.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lina Khan </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/704af780-85dd-4a73-8331-32f4cd15d135?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">has also written</a><span> that “There are no such things as market ‘forces’.” Statements like this certainly don’t do much to refute Chait’s allegation that the antimonopoly belief system “is more like a religion than an economic theory”. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First of all, as an aside, we should consider what it would mean for market forces not to exist and prices to be determined by politics. It would mean that grocery stores carefully calculate exactly how much they can charge for a cucumber or a package of napkins without Senators giving them an angry call or the working class rioting, or something like that. That’s kind of preposterous. It would also mean that small businesses would charge </span><em>lower</em><span> prices, because they’re less politically powerful than big businesses. But in fact, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/acc29bac-1ec9-44e6-87e9-782a1a840aef?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">it’s big businesses that charge lower prices</a><span> for the same goods. So the “prices are determined by politics” idea is just abjectly ridiculous, except maybe in a few special cases or where explicit regulation is involved. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But more to the point: Market forces obviously </span><em>do</em><span> exist. When you </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2baf9e86-1112-4ed1-b74c-ff841ffe3317?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">include sales taxes on price tags</a><span> — reminding people that prices are higher than they had thought — they buy less, proving that demand curves exist and slope downward. When there is bad weather at sea, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0d557df0-76da-40ee-96ab-1ba36afb4735?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the price of fish goes up</a><span>. When you charge electricity customers more, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6c770b05-5cee-41ee-86f2-5e0e797f8042?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">they use less electricity</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And so on. Market forces are not easy to observe in all cases, and they’re not always the most important determinant of prices. But their existence has been proven so thoroughly, by so much careful empirical observation, that to deny their existence requires a deep level of mysticism and blind faith. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re not the kind of person to believe in empirical economics, then of course you’re not going to care if economists find evidence against your worldview. But once we move out of the realm of willful faith-based belief and into the real world of evidence and observation, we find that the science on monopoly power is far from settled.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">First of all, there is the evidence I cited before about decreasing concentration in local labor markets (even as concentration increases nationwide). The monopsony wage penalty might be very high, but it was probably even higher in the past; this leaves room for antitrust action to help workers, but it should make us question whether monopoly power is at the root of slow wage growth.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But more fundamentally, the entire story about creeping market power being responsible for a bunch of different ills in the modern American economy is </span><em>under serious dispute</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, the whole story about monopoly power increasing in recent decades relies on the idea that </span><em>price markups have increased</em><span> — if companies can’t charge higher prices relative to their costs, they must not be very powerful. Economists like De Loecker and Eeckhout find that markups have increased a lot, but there are plenty of economists who disagree with that finding! There are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c9ed95de-bf0d-4d06-936f-fd2afa0b4c4e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">tons of measurement issues</a><span> involved in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/72187044-a066-43e9-9426-77717799bdb4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">trying to estimate</a><span> markups across the whole economy. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dec05a58-f0d2-4aaf-bc36-2f5653273e09?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Some economists claim</a><span> that essentially the entire increase in markups is due to the finance sector. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are plenty of other pieces of the monopoly power story that are also disputed. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a5e1fea2-7b08-4078-850e-897c1555a377?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Shapiro and Yurukoglu (2024)</a><span> summarize a bunch of these. It’s hard to define what each “market” is over time, because the boundaries of the categories are arbitrary, and the nature of products themselves keeps changing. It’s hard to choose the region over which local concentration should be measured (when is one store in the same “market” as another?). Companies’ costs are hard to measure for many reasons — for example, companies sell lots of different things, and researchers don’t necessarily have the data to determine which costs are for which products. Profits are hard to measure because the cost of risk is hard to assess. And so on. In general, choosing a different set of assumptions can get you wildly different results regarding how much monopoly power has actually risen in America.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The point here is not that De Loecker and Eeckhout, or the other economists who concluded in the 2010s that monopoly power is a big deal, were </span><em>wrong</em><span>. Maybe they were, maybe they weren’t. Nor should you conclude that economics is just a game of “he said, she said” where everyone contradicts each other and nobody really knows anything. The correct takeaway here is that these questions are very subtle and difficult, and the most careful, serious researchers will take a long time to hash out the correct answer. In the meantime, </span><strong>we must live with uncertainty</strong><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A big problem with the antimonopoly crusaders is that they don’t just refuse to live with uncertainty — they </span><em>insist that you don’t live with uncertainty</em><span> either. If you say “Hey dudes, maybe corporate landlords actually lower rents”, they won’t debate the finer points of causal estimation with you — they’ll simply label you as a corporate shill and dismiss you.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Don’t let the factionalists win</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s this last bit — the anathematization of anyone who disagrees with them — that really warns me away from the antimonopoly movement. Chait describes in his article how anyone who tries to buck the antimonopoly people gets accused of being a paid corporate hack:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We’ve largely won the intellectual debate,” [Lynn] told me matter-of-factly, allowing that the only remaining liberals who disagree with him are “</span><strong>those who are paid to do so</strong><span>.”…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When Biden considered appointing Susan Davies, a former deputy White House counsel under President Obama, to the Justice Department’s top antitrust post, a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cccbb869-bcce-4dd4-97f1-e5a564239eda?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">slew</a><span> of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/959ac095-5ce4-4519-b913-af8e26947c67?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">articles</a><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2733e8d8-ca9b-4230-9753-fa296e519b7d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">savaged</a><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b2484a16-5c33-472f-83ad-c658759be3d6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">her</a><span> as </span><strong>a corporate shill</strong><span>. Her candidacy died. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This tactic was clearly on display when the antimonopoly people leapt to savage Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s book </span><em>Abundance</em><span>. Matt Stoller </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6f7ab530-73e8-4208-b7fa-b85d8276948a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">wrote a post</a><span> entitled “An Abundance of Sleaze: How a Beltway Brain Trust Sells Oligarchy to Liberals”. Dylan Gyauch-Lewis</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a0aa6ec7-52a8-4ad1-8e4a-87c4c3568141?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">called the Abundance movement</a><span> “The new centrist push to regain control of the Democratic Party, with corporate money”. Barry C. Lynn said that Abundance wants “to cozy up to good oligarchs, so they can shelter us until the MAGA storm blows over.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">First of all, claiming that anyone who disagrees with your ideas must be on the payroll of nefarious forces is blatant intellectual dishonesty. It also signals how weak your argument is if you have to accuse every critic of being a bad actor. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But beyond that, the antimonopoly crusaders’ reaction to </span><em>Abundance</em><span> shows how utterly </span><em>factionalist</em><span> they are. They could have simply said “Yes, we want abundance too. Guess how you get abundance? By breaking up monopolies!” Or something like that. They could have easily tried to co-opt the energy behind </span><em>Abundance</em><span> and treated Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson as potential allies. Instead, they leapt instantly to the attack with maximum savagery. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the behavior of factionalists, for whom ideas and policy are less important than building power for a clique of favored allies and fellow-travelers within the Democratic Party. Klein and Thompson were a threat not because their ideas contradicted those of the antimonopoly clique, but simply because </span><em>they were not beholden</em><span> to the patronage or the intellectual legacy of that clique. They were not on the team, so they were the enemy. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In my view, it is very dangerous for any political party to allow itself to be entered and captured by a clique or faction like this. I’ve spent a long time being very favorable to the </span><em>ideas</em><span> being put forward by the antimonopoly people, but their </span><em>behavior</em><span> with regards to the Abundance liberals — and the shoddy reasoning, baseless accusations, and backroom arm-twisting that they employ in these debates — has given me what the Zoomers call “the ick”. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A problem with economic policy is that it is very vulnerable to </span><em>intellectual pseudo-cults</em><span>. Economics research is very hard to understand, isn’t always useful, and rarely offers clear-cut answers. So policymakers and writers seeking certainty and a reason for decisiveness often fall victim to charismatic gangs of intellectuals who claim that economics is solved and that they have it all figured out. On the GOP side, these include the “supply-siders” in the 1980s and the “national conservatives” today. On the Democratic side, it includes </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0c4fb8f-2a76-437e-8fb9-b9ebb024ce3f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the MMT people</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But MMT failed — essentially no one listens to people who say infinite deficits are good. The antimonopoly faction, on the other hand, appears to have succeeded in winning enormous power and prestige within an increasingly epistemically closed progressive movement. Elizabeth Warren was basically a one-woman Organization Department</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">²</span><span> for the Biden administration, popular Democrats like AOC are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c0435c97-4adf-45cb-b32d-95b60c4819a8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">going around claiming</a><span> that “market power” is what produces billionaires, and every major progressive publication now platforms their intellectual output. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Given my writings about the problems of corporate power in the past — and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45501f90-bb41-430d-86d1-1fd037c4c35f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">my fear of the overwhelming power</a><span> that AI companies might achieve — it would be relatively easy for me to join this movement. But I can’t, because monomaniacal obsession, epistemic closure, anti-empiricism, and intense factionalism are the kinds of things I just can’t sign on to. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Corporate power </span><em>is</em><span> a real problem in our society. But we need more reasonable programs, and more reasonable </span><em>people</em><span>, to fight it effectively. Banning corporate landlords, calling for </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/95a27648-963f-4cb8-b33d-e015c83c3fbb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">price controls</a><span>, attacking the grocery store industry, forcing airlines out of business, and making accusations against anyone who calls for deregulation of housing supply are just signs of an approach that’s going to lead nowhere good. </span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;">We’ve had to put up with a lot when it comes to AI. From taking people’s clothes off on Twitter to helping kids cheat on tests to producing fruit dramas we can’t stop watching (just me?), the haters have plenty to complain about. But if AI could cure cancer, the holy grail of biotech, would all the other bullshit be worth it? And perhaps, more interestingly, would an AI that was powerful enough to cure cancer be an AI we would even want to live alongside?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These were the kinds of questions that Jerusalem dug into with Staff Writer Kelsey Piper at a recent live debate held by</span><em> The Argument</em><span> in San Francisco. The marquee read: Can AI Cure Cancer? Ultimately, it was a debate about what realistically we could expect from LLMs and what “curing cancer” would even look like.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Kelsey is an optimist but not a maximalist. </p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #04B2A5;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“I see a billboard. It’s like, ‘Here’s cloud infrastructure balancing.’ Is cloud infrastructure balancing going to cure cancer? No, but it’s good … The world is good because of lots of things that are small and make something a little bit better.” </p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">What she expects is that we will continue curing cancer at roughly the rate of the last 40 years. For Kelsey, the problem is that LLMs are good at verifiable tasks, and cancer biology is full of unverifiable ones. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the definition of curing cancer with AI changes depending on who you ask. When Google’s Demis Hassabis says AlphaFold will one day cure cancer, he’s referring to AI tools that can speed up protein prediction and drug discovery. AlphaFold doesn’t work like the typical LLM or promise a magic cancer-curing pill, but it could allow us to gradually develop therapeutics.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, meanwhile, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/83ec66e3-28fe-4f39-ba5a-550868d84386?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">shared</a><span> a story about a man who treated his dog’s cancer, claiming it was cured with a personalized drug developed with assistance from ChatGPT. ChatGPT didn’t actually make the drug or cure the dog, but it was able to help the dog’s owner find the right people, machines, and techniques to treat his pet and extend its life.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And when Anthropic’s Dario Amodei talks about curing cancer, he’s relying on recursive self-improvement: a model that trains a better model until you have something so capable that it solves everything. To paraphrase Kelsey: If you asked Claude to build God to cure cancer, you could end up with an AI so powerful that Claude itself would suggest you don’t do it. (Whether or not a God-like AI is a good idea, it does sound like I’d win the debate in that scenario.)</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em>The Argument </em><span>will be back next week with a regular Matt-and-Jerusalem episode.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>The transcript will be after the paywall in this post for paying subscribers.</strong></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Announcer: </strong><span>Please welcome Jerusalem Demsas and Kelsey Piper.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas:</strong><span> All right. And, again, that’s a second compliment I’m giving Elon.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But it is the case that, just as an observational matter, like, I witness people all the time just asking Grok if something is true. I have no idea if their epistemics change, but they do stop arguing after they’re told repeatedly that they’re incorrect about something, and they’re always presented with one version of the facts. And there’s something structural...</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I mean, you did an experiment for us testing AI models in multiple different languages and finding out that they’re all, like, libbed out because they’re all trained on, like, words, which Libs wrote, so…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper: </strong><span>They’re broadly big on individual freedom and choice and...</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>So, Kelsey, did, and we hired translators from multiple different languages, and I don’t know if you wanna explain it:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper: </strong><span>So, I was imagining, I was curious whether, like, if I ask in Arabic if it is wrong for me to be gay or whatever, if it gives a different answer than it does in English. It doesn’t. I think this is because, as far as I can tell, a lot of the frontier models reason in English regardless, and then just answer in whatever language.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But, anyway, the values that they have, which are broadly the small-L liberal values — they’re pretty in favor of individual rights and individual freedom. They’re in favor of...</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>Yeah. They’re like, “Should I be mad that my kid came out?” It’s like, “No, you should not.” And it’s like, it doesn’t matter if it’s in Arabic or in Hindi or in Chinese. And I was like, “Wow, this is total lib domination through AI.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And so, I’m not 100% certain about this, but I am more bullish than I think other people are…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper: </strong><span>That</span><strong> </strong><span>they’re good for the information environment on social media?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>Yeah, which I think is a huge problem for democracies if you don’t have that ability to have a place where people can go. And I do think, like, lots of people are using it, even if they’re telling pollsters sometimes they don’t trust it, they are using it to get information. They’re using it all the time to get information about what’s going on in the world and what they should do, and basic facts they were googling beforehand.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The other thing… I mean, other major problems… </span><br><br><span>I mean, I started a company last year — theargumentmag.com. I have to; I was told once I don’t promote it enough. So now I’m becoming like a bot — but, you know, I started the company last year, and I cannot express how much I don’t think I could have really done it without A) Hiring more people and having more lawyers and paying more legal fees, if I didn’t have Claude.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And, one thing that I’ve learned — especially from, you know, family members who are from different countries with with less resources — it’s just, the speed at which it can make you capable of something that might feel very normal in the U.S., like, now is possible in Ethiopia or Eritrea or wherever — like, you know, these places I’m familiar with. And it’s just like, you know, entrepreneurship is one of the defining characteristics of the United States that has made it often better at achieving economic growth.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And, I mean, if you’re able to just skyrocket the number of people who can start their own enterprises, I think that will look very big on economic growth statistics. We’re already seeing lots of change in productivity statistics. Like, that, I think, is a big problem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But, you know, as you’ll note, I don’t think either of us have mentioned some other… I mean, you know, OpenAI seems, the foundation seems, bullish on the idea of solving Alzheimer’s, too, through AI because I think there are very promising proteins — that there are genes that they’re targeting — so, that’s another place where I feel like there’s some hope.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper: </strong><span>So, in the long run, I think we’re going to continue making scientific progress. And we can debate whether it’s going to be like a sudden jump due to a few huge blockbuster discoveries or more, you know, continuing to get the results that we have been. Like, the last 50 years have been a series of triumphs over cancer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They’ve been incomplete and partial, but they’ve gotten better. I’m pro-progress, I’m pro-growth. I want to see all of that continue. I don’t want to do the “country of geniuses in a data center” plan. I think that plan is a bad idea. But if we’re not doing that plan, I’m broadly willing to let human beings individually discover what powerful tools at their disposal let them do. Like, that is my inclination.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But I think if you’re going to specifically promise, you know, that you’re going to deliver these results. And then, in fact, it’s the case that the specialized RL systems, the alpha fold and programs like it for finding specific proteins, if that is where all the action is, and the large language models are not related, I think that’s kind of important to a lot of people’s views on this.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Like, if the AI that’s curing cancer is the AlphaFold stuff, then it’s, to my mind, more reason we don’t need to go try and do the “geniuses in data centers” plan and can focus on the pure RL.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So, related to that, one of the questions was like, “If RL gets better at nonverifiable responses and just generally cheaper and faster and better with that kink you’re thinking about this, and like, I’m already pretty pro-AlphaFold and all of that stuff. But yes, obviously, if we continue seeing huge growth there, that’s a big deal.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>So, another question we got a couple of times is like, “All right guys, you said you didn’t want to put your money where your mouth is, but you really should because that’s embarrassing. And I think that that’s true.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper: </strong><span>How much do we expect cancer to fall in the next 10 years...</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>I think us throwing out numbers is maybe not a good idea right now, but I think what we should probably do is just, we should put this on the website, just like what our numbers would be. And I think that, like, using the benchmark of what mortality rates are.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper: </strong><span>Maybe if people live longer, they die of cancer. Like, part of the problem here is that a lot of this is a bet on differential progress between cancer and other things that kill you. Like, I have...</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas:</strong><span> Even if we create God, we still will die. Yes, correct.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper: </strong><span>Probably.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas:</strong><span> I mean, I do think, though, that one really promising sign… because, like, one of the critiques of whether or not we’re going to cure cancer is that, you know, you get really much better at diagnosis, but all you’ve done is actually get… You know, you’ve diagnosed someone earlier, and so your survival rates look like they’ve gone up. But really, you just found out earlier, so of course your five-year survival rate...</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper:</strong><span> Oh God, country comparisons are such a nightmare for this reason. I was trying to determine definitively who has the best health care system. And I was thinking the easiest way to do this is to look at something that kills people at about the same rate across a bunch of different places or occurs naturally in the population at about the same rate, and then see who does the best job of curing it, and then I will have my answer once and for all.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And then, I learned why no one else has done this, which is that, yeah, everybody defines everything completely differently from each other. Everybody had, like even… Everybody’s populations are different ages, which affects a lot of things, and different backgrounds, which affects a lot of things.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And even if you meticulously control for all of that, those are probably only the most visible proxies for a bunch of other invisible stuff that affects people’s rate of getting everything.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>So, you didn’t solve that question?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper:</strong><span> Oh, I solved it by deciding that I’d been right, and…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>Well, I mean, but I think that one reason why we shouldn’t be so… just decide that it’s, like, impossible to know if we’ve actually cured some cancers, is that, when you look at the Massai trial that happened recently, found that interval cancer — so, like, often, the cancers that are, you know, after someone’s gotten diagnosed and then treated and then they’re in remission, and like, the one that gets you is the one that you forget to catch in between.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And, like, that’s really aggressive. And we saw those going down significantly because of: Just diagnosis got better. And so, to me, that’s a sign that you are going to be able to get progress here, even if, eventually, yes, we all do die.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper:</strong><span> Well, and there has been enormous progress. Like, at one point, I wanted to do slides and then it turned out to be too complicated — by which I mean, not the venue; they were great. The part where I had to make all of the slides was too complicated — but just showing there’s so many cancers...</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>You know, Claude can do that.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Kelsey Piper:</strong><span> I have an uncle who had cancer as a child, and the treatment left him disabled for life. He survived, but the radiation just did a bunch of damage to his body. These days, you would be walking; bounce back in full health in six months. And I know other people who died of cancers as young children — well, I don’t know the people who died; I know their relatives — that now we have a cure for.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We have made incredible progress on this. And I do think that that progress isn’t over, even if I’m not sure whether to expect it to speed up.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Jerusalem Demsas: </strong><span>OK. Well, we have not completely resolved every question, but I think this is a great place to close. And what I’ll let you guys know is that we’re going to be around for the next hour or so. So, please come up to us, ask your questions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;">But thank you for being our first live event in San Francisco!</p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Fourteen months ago, Donald Trump announced that he was starting a trade war by imposing sweeping tariffs on almost every nation in the world. His move caused shock waves, and not just because of the economic impact.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The Trump tariffs were clearly illegal — taxes imposed not via proper legislation, but by invoking an obscure existing law intended to deal with economic emergencies, even though no emergency existed. Also, by imposing these tariffs unilaterally, Trump was violating many decades’ worth of solemn U.S. agreements with other nations, including our closest allies. So “Liberation Day” marked the end of rule of law at home — goodbye separation of powers, hello a monarchical system in which the president does whatever he wants. And it also marked the transformation of the United States into a rogue nation that holds its erstwhile allies in contempt and can’t be trusted to honor its promises.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The initial shock has faded, largely because there have been so many outrages since, from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2273a425-7e55-4297-a532-37fe928b1266?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">pogroms</a><span> at home to the disastrous war in Iran. And the Supreme Court, after dragging its feet for many months, eventually, grudgingly, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4c9219e1-632e-4947-8df6-6afd7f1e7cf8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">ruled</a><span> that the illegal tariffs were, in fact, illegal, and will have to be refunded.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But Trump officials kept many of the tariffs in place using </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5cc61e47-370a-44b5-b5b0-291accf82998?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">another obscure law</a><span>, this one intended to deal with balance of payments emergencies, although again no such emergency existed. This invocation of “Section 122” will probably also be ruled illegal at some point, but in any case the law sets a 150-day time limit on such tariffs, so the Trumpists needed another dodge.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Yesterday it came in the form of “Section 301” tariffs on 60 trading partners, including the European Union and Japan. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c394012c-6a10-473e-93c0-8c60d098c652?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Section 301</a><span> is titled “Relief from Unfair Trade Practices.” So what are the unfair practices the Trumpists say the whole world is engaging in?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The answer is that the Trump administration is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/172f0e3f-2597-4510-b61f-18375156933f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">accusing</a><span> other countries of “failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Notice the wording. They aren’t accusing the European Union itself of employing slave labor. Even the Trumpists aren’t willing to lie that shamelessly (yet). No, the claim is that the EU isn’t doing enough to stop countries that do employ slave labor from selling their goods in Europe.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Everyone, and I mean everyone, understands that the alleged justification for these tariffs is a lie. There is absolutely no reason to believe that the EU is less diligent about opposing the use of slave labor than the US. For that matter, there is no reason to believe that Trump and his minions have any particular objection to slave labor. This is nothing but a transparently, one might say sneeringly, bogus rationale for continuing to flout both US law and international agreements.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why do Trump’s minions keep using legal tricks and lies to impose tariffs? There is, after all, no reason they couldn’t simply ask Congress to impose tariffs through normal legislation. But doing so would run into three problems, from Trump’s point of view. First, Congress might balk. Second, at minimum an attempt to pass legislation would require hearings, in which the weakness of the administration’s arguments would become obvious. Third, one of the reasons Trump loves tariffs is that he gets to issue decrees at will, none of this pesky nonsense of consulting with the legislative branch; having to follow the Constitution would spoil his fantasies of omnipotence.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So here we go again, with another round of tariffs that will probably be ruled illegal some months from now.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Why doesn’t Trump just back down? After all, the tariffs aren’t achieving their stated objectives. Remember how Trump was going to revive US manufacturing?</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: And we’re already seeing things like a $50 million push not just to help Democrats win races in the midterms, but specifically to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/646d129c-7763-4599-8711-f8e59898d3f5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">get their campaigns to center child care issues</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Elizabeth Warren, a critically important thought-leader in the party, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5f2bc11a-f6e6-4780-b691-6284e992643d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">said at the Center for American Progress’s IDEAS Conference in May</a><span> that “It would be political malpractice for Democrats not to be talking about child care every chance we get, going into the midterms and beyond.” </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But of course, she doesn’t just want to talk about child care in the abstract. She wants to talk specifically about her Child Care for Every Community Act, which was introduced last year with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/370e61b6-453f-45dc-9863-186397ec2261?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Mikie Sherrill as House co-sponsor</a><span>, a role that has been </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/091f2e66-2116-4374-8054-ccbc62de3e11?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">taken up by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez</a><span> now that Sherrill is governor of New Jersey. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The link between calling on Democrats to campaign on an issue and pushing specific policy measures relates to a very dysfunctional norm in the Democratic Party where everyone more or less agrees that the way to win a substantive argument about policy prioritization is to first win an argument about messaging. There’s a similar push underway, led by Sheldon Whitehouse, to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f23c97f0-3d55-4f64-9411-7483968304d3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">get Democrats to talk more about climate change</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, for senators like Warren and Whitehouse with safe seats in New England, there’s no downside to just talking about both. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Democrats need to win races in Iowa and Alaska and Texas and Ohio if they’re going to do anything at all. And to do that, it helps for the national party to have accurate information about what voters care about. But if progressive issue advocates believe that the only way to secure prioritization for their topic is to deceive party elites about the voters’ priorities, they’re incentivized to engage in spreading misinformation. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I would note that you don’t actually </span><em>need</em><span> to conduct politics this way. In 2001 and then again in 2003 and again in 2017 and </span><em>again</em><span> in 2025, newly elected Republican presidents prioritized regressive tax cuts that conservatives believe are morally important. But Republicans have never made “we want to cut rich people’s taxes” the centerpiece of a national political campaign. They don’t even make it the centerpiece of their pitch for the regressive tax bills they promote. They simply keep in mind that the thing </span><em>they</em><span> most care about is not the same as the thing that </span><em>persuadable voters </em><span>most care about. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And just as persuadable voters </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/171dcdbb-8e23-413c-ae84-8b5b6d1c45fd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">don’t really care about climate change</a><span>, they don’t seem to care very much about child care either. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I don’t want to get the people at Navigator Research in trouble, because they’re trying to be good Democrats and progressive allies. But </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/33c4f90a-70f7-4eb9-98da-bf2ed6cf6ccb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">their latest battleground polling presentation</a><span> (which to be clear is full of good news for Dems) also makes it clear that the child care issue is a niche topic. </span></p><div Child care costs are a huge topic for dual-income couples with kids under five, especially if they live in expensive metro areas. But while people like that are very well-represented in the Democratic Party staffer class, they’re just not a very large share of the population. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Interest in subsidized day care centers is limited </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One issue here is just that while the general topic of child care is highly salient to anyone whose kids are too young for public school, that’s just not that many people. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f58ef5d8-b7b0-4c6f-b24a-6fb6016e93c1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">As I wrote back during the 2020 primary, </a><span>Democrats were looking at this issue through a very particular lens. The kinds of people who become members of Congress or who run for president or who work on political campaigns or in the media or for policy advocacy organizations tend to be really into their jobs. These are lines of work where people typically earn less money than someone with their skills or credentials could earn in the corporate sector. And because this work has a lot of intrinsic appeal to a highly motivated subset of the population, the jobs are difficult to obtain even though they don’t pay very well. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">People like that who are also politically progressive — especially if they are politically progressive women — have a very specific concern about their careers getting derailed by family responsibilities. They also tend to have nine-to-five, Monday-Friday jobs rather than working odd hours in service industries. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If that’s you, then formal center-based child care (i.e., things like day care centers and preschools) is a good solution, especially if that means high-quality facilities with trained staff. It is, however, very expensive, especially in generally high-cost metro areas. But even though it can seem like “everyone” is worried about this, it’s actually a somewhat idiosyncratic preoccupation of media and political professionals in D.C. and New York. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>New America, a center-left organization, recently surveyed parents with kids under five, and they found that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/01e5f741-b875-488f-acee-3143cf17fd4d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">desire to spend more time with kids</a><span> is much more common than desire to spend more time at work. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think there is probably some social desirability bias at work here — who’s going to say no to “quality time” with your kids? But the fact that paid work ranks below things like “household tasks” and “personal time” is a reminder that way more people have jobs than careers. They’re working for money, not self-actualization. </p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most people are not parents of young kids, so </span><em>any</em><span> proposal to spend lots of money specifically on parents of young kids is something of an uphill climb. The particular version of center-based care with standards modeled on Head Start and military child care programs </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b776e0b8-2219-47d0-b534-2d7c9ac6f286?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">that Elizabeth Warren and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have landed on</a><span> compounds the problem because it offers something most parents of young kids don’t particularly want. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Program design details matter</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Somewhat separate from the politics, it’s also worth paying attention to what exactly this proposed program does. Building on proposals from the 2020 presidential campaigns and early iterations of Build Back Better, the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/370e61b6-453f-45dc-9863-186397ec2261?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Warren bill</a><span> says that “higher-income families would pay no more than 7 percent of their income, while lower-income families making less than 75 percent of their state median income would be fully subsidized.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This kind of sliding-scale rather than universal approach helps keep down the headline cost of the program. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it does also mean that as designed, the bill does the </span><em>least</em><span> for the kind of upscale married professional women who are the target constituency for full-time center-based care. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Warren’s program would give a much larger boost to working-class parents, many of whom would probably prefer to use additional financial resources to cut back on working hours. There’s a big risk that by subsidizing a lot of families who are not currently in the center-based child care market (because they’re relying on more informal arrangements) to enter it, you wind up pushing the unsubsidized price up quite a bit and somewhat backfiring on the people who’d be most inclined to like this idea. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is exacerbated by the fact that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/370e61b6-453f-45dc-9863-186397ec2261?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">the program</a><span> is, of course, a bit of an everything bagel that “ensures parity by requiring that wages and benefits for child care workers be comparable to those of similarly credentialed local public-school teachers.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I will confess that I do not completely understand what that means, since most child-care-center workers have different credentials from local public-school teachers. But the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees — which has endorsed the legislation — has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73317f75-9a06-41d9-bbfe-2efa6499d9b7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">an initiative</a><span> where the </span><em>owners</em><span> of subsidized day care centers in California unionize to collectively bargain for higher reimbursement rates from the state. </span></p><div Child care is not a salient issue for the mass public, and parents of young kids are divided on the extent to which this is their preferred child care arrangement. But unlike cash assistance, it has a specific interest-group coalition behind it. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Look for smaller ways to help</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Getting back to where we started, Democrats should try to run in 2026 and 2028 on messages that appeal to voters’ actual priorities rather than letting issue advocates gaslight them into thinking that climate change </span><em>or</em><span> child care is really driving the electorate. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Separately from that, Democrats at an elite level need to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0bd08f67-4140-4a57-a7a1-b5f57fada766?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">try to do some priority-setting</a><span> based on what they actually think is important. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re going to spend a bunch of money on something child-related that the voters aren’t particularly clamoring for, I think it makes a lot more sense to focus on expanding the Child Tax Credit (perhaps specifically for kids too young for kindergarten) than on this interest-group slop. Parents could use the money to pay for child care at day care centers, but they could also use it to help out in other ways. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s worth emphasizing here that family expenses don’t fall into neat little buckets. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are good ideas to reduce housing costs that focus on land use, mortgage regulation, and other regulatory barriers to supply and that don’t cost any money. If housing were cheaper, that would make raising a family more affordable, even if those reforms aren’t specifically targeted at child care costs. The easiest thing Democrats can do to make center-based child care specifically more affordable is to look at regulatory issues. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dfad75ec-36ce-4acd-be9e-6d1a34bc4a87?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Devon Gorry and Diana Weinert Thomas find</a><span> that the lower day care staffing ratios in blue states raise costs despite no clear evidence of improving quality. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On an even more low-profile level, one of the few immigration restrictionist measures undertaken by the Biden administration was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/460e8204-b28b-4f3b-919d-c37f19d9ac2b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">tighter regulation of the au pair program</a><span>, which the Trump administration has also handicapped by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1138b2f3-9d88-45c3-85d6-3e88596e1d1b?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">screwing around with visa administration</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It seems like trying to encourage orderly and relatively uncontroversial forms of immigration like au pairs is a much better idea than going wobbly on border enforcement or deportations of people who get arrested. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But this all hinges on actually prioritizing the interests of consumers of child care services rather than viewing subsidies to the child care sector as a jobs program. </p><p class="button-wrapper" And in August Trump held a meeting with Vladimir Putin in which, as the Russians see it, he offered to broker a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/aadf296f-b518-4e1b-9bde-347fad88c2a2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">deal</a><span> that would give Russia control of a crucial fortress belt on Ukrainian soil.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was a shocking betrayal of a democracy fighting for its freedom — and, in so doing, fighting for the freedom of Europe as a whole. Even some Republicans are ashamed. Yesterday 18 Republican members of the House </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b7235dd8-3c68-4663-9b3f-36ed3b4f6172?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">broke ranks</a><span> with their leadership and voted for a bill that would restore aid to Ukraine and impose sanctions on Russia. But the bill has no chance of becoming law, because Trump is siding ever closely more with Putin in a war that is now well into its fifth year.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But a funny thing happened to Trump’s attempt to hand Ukraine over to his comrade in thuggery: the war has turned in Ukraine’s favor. The fighting remains a gruesome slugfest, but Ukraine’s superior flexibility and capacity for innovation have gradually given it the upper hand in the drone warfare that increasingly shapes combat. In fact, Ukraine is so proficient at drone warfare that the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Saudi Arabia — which are facing drone attacks as a consequence of Trump’s disastrous Iran war — have </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1ce368ab-1a6f-4af4-b17a-929df53e7eca?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">signed agreements</a><span> to draw on Ukrainian technology and expertise.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Zelenskyy, it turns out, does have quite a few cards, while Trump has far fewer cards than he imagined.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Before Trump, we were also a nation almost universally regarded as essential: Nations believed that they needed access to U.S. banks to do business, access to U.S. markets to prosper, access to U.S. weapons to defend themselves. But by breaking decades’ worth of international agreements — not to mention threatening allies and betraying Ukraine — Trump quickly forfeited the world’s trust. By failing so spectacularly against Iran, a far weaker military power, Trump has dispelled much of the world’s fear.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And now the fact that the world is managing economically despite Trump’s tariffs, while Ukraine is surviving despite Trump’s attempt to cut it off at the knees, has revealed that we are much less essential than everyone assumed.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">NONMUSICAL CODA</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">June 5, 1944 — back when we were a reliable and essential ally of nations fighting for freedom.</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/76a9c5f5-7c4d-408a-bdb8-e43ecd54d4be?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/SOZUB0EHadw" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/85f4dd59-68a4-47f8-be95-12e679a8e058?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;">Mint Images</a><span> via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At WelcomeFest earlier this week, I was pleased to moderate a panel with Representatives Adam Gray and Tom Suozzi — the only two House Democrats to have flipped Trump districts in 2024 — where they </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ca4b146c-043e-4d00-a43a-c795f169cf2a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">unveiled the Promise to America</a><span>, which is a kind of moderate Democrat manifesto. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The idea here is to try to transcend </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/190bd822-4edf-4726-9812-dbe3b37100c0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">dog-whistle moderation</a><span> and the tendency of strong electoral performers to want to just be independent thinkers focused on their districts and eschew playing for a team. Part of the issue is that while electoral pragmatism is important, pragmatism alone doesn’t really provide you with a framework for governing. It also doesn’t help you find like-minded people and build pipelines and networks that extend across multiple states, multiple kinds of roles, and endure. The basic idea is that they want people who broadly agree with the principles outlined to sign the Promise and ideally build a large team of officeholders and candidates and ordinary citizens who like these ideas. </span></p><div class="subscription-widget-wrap" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="subscription-widget show-subscribe" style="font-size: 16px;direction: ltr !important;font-weight: 400;text-decoration: none;font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';color: #363737;line-height: 1.5;max-width: 560px;margin: 24px auto;align-items: flex-start;display: block;text-align: center;padding: 0px 32px;"><div class="preamble" style="margin-top: 16px;font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-size: 18px;max-width: 384px;width: fit-content;line-height: 22px;display: flex;align-items: center;text-align: center;font-weight: 400;margin-left: auto;margin-right: auto;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Mailbag answers are for everyone, but the questions below came from paid subscribers.
